anti_overlap: Do not cover PRD format quality (problem statement, solution prose, Goals section) — that belongs to fd-prd-quality-standard
Do not cover the product-management meta-question of whether the right items are deferred — that belongs to fd-pm-decomposition-discipline
Do not cover whether individual acceptance criteria are measurable and testable — that belongs to fd-acceptance-criteria-precision
decision_lens: The right decomposition is the one where each feature has a single decision-maker, a single risk profile, and a single dependency ceiling. When a feature bundles a policy decision with an implementation, the policy decision's unresolved risk blocks the implementation's completed work. When a feature's dependency is listed as 'needs the previous feature' but the dependency is actually only on one sub-deliverable of the previous feature, the dependency overstates the blocking relationship and inflates the critical path.
focus: Whether F1/F2/F3/F4 are the right features in the right shape: hidden load-bearing decisions inside 'implementation detail,' incorrect dependency ordering, candidates for splitting or merging, and bundling that inflates the critical path
name: fd-feature-decomposition-shape
persona: Apply the perspective of a delivery-focused tech lead who reviews PRD decompositions before planning, has seen migration PRDs where the bundling of a policy-design subfeature with a code-change subfeature caused the code change to sit unreleased for weeks, and has developed a systematic approach to identifying where 'one feature' is actually two features with different risk profiles, different required expertise, and different dependency ceilings.
review_areas: F4 is explicitly named as 'two parts' — F4a (selective cache invalidation) and F4b (event-log stratification). F4a is a code correctness change with clear acceptance criteria (three specific test cases, existing tests pass). F4b is a policy-design-plus-implementation-plus-benchmark. F4a depends only on Phase 1's DerivationDecl.reads; F4b depends additionally on F3's identity-constitutive event class. These two sub-features have different dependency ceilings: F4a can begin (and close) as soon as F1 is done; F4b cannot close until F3 is done. Bundling them means the migration epic cannot open until F4b closes, even if F4a closed weeks earlier — unnecessarily extending the critical path.

F3's dependency structure is stated as 'independent of F1, can run in parallel after F1 opens the workspace.' But F3's document deliverables — the decision document, the brainstorm audit, the Open Question update — have no dependency on the workspace topology. Only F3's yangsi branch's recognition-test definition might reference the actual codebase (to name which SoulEvent kinds exist). F3 could begin on day one without waiting for F1. The dependency diagram is overly conservative and will cause F3 to start later than necessary.

F1's acceptance criteria include updating 'the brainstorm's Decisions table to record the chosen shape.' This is a documentation deliverable that does not need to be gated on the cargo check passing — the decision can be documented before the topology is verified, and the documentation update is not itself on the critical path for unblocking F2/F3. Mixing a documentation deliverable with a code verification criterion in the same acceptance criterion list obscures which criterion is actually the gate for unblocking the next feature.

F2's yes-path (countries are Souls) and no-path (countries are not Souls) are presented as alternative completions of the same feature. But the yes-path produces a spec (aggregation operator) that is an input to Palettice Phase 2 design; the no-path produces a definitional statement that closes a scoping question. These outputs serve different downstream consumers and have different quality standards. Treating them as one feature means the quality bar for the yes-path spec is only implicitly higher — it should be explicit.

The PRD's dependency section shows F2 and F3 as parallel children of F1 and F4 as a child of F3. This is the dependency of the code deliverables. But the document deliverables of F2 and F3 have no dependency on F1 at all. A more precise dependency diagram would show: document deliverables of F1/F2/F3 as parallel (no dependencies between them); topology verification of F1 as a gate for the migration epic; F4a as a child of F1 topology; F4b as a child of F3 (identity-constitutive event class) and F4a (shared infrastructure). This representation would shorten the critical path and allow document work to begin immediately.

severity_examples.condition: F4a's cache invalidation code change is straightforward and could close quickly. Bundled with F4b, it cannot be closed until the stratification policy design is complete, the schema migration is tested, and the benchmark is written. The migration epic's open gate is held by F4b's slowest work item even after F4a is done.
severity_examples.scenario: F4a blocked by F4b's unresolved policy design

severity_examples.condition: If planning treats F3 as blocked on F1 completion (because the dependency diagram shows F3 as a child of F1), the document-only deliverables of F3 (decision document, brainstorm audit) will not begin until F1 closes. F1's topology verification may take longer than expected; F3's document work would sit idle unnecessarily.
severity_examples.scenario: F3 delayed by overstatement of F1 dependency

severity_examples.condition: If F2 resolves to yes (countries are Souls), the aggregation operator spec becomes an input to Palettice Phase 2 design and must meet a higher quality bar than F2's no-path definitional paragraph. Without naming the quality bar for the yes-path spec, the F2 feature can close with an underspecified aggregation operator that forces a redesign when Phase 2 opens.
severity_examples.scenario: F2 yes-path spec quality bar undefined relative to no-path

success_hints: For each feature, identify whether it contains a policy-design subfeature and a code-change subfeature with different dependency ceilings, and whether splitting them would shorten the critical path
Map the actual dependencies of each sub-deliverable (not the whole feature) and check whether the stated feature-level dependency is the binding constraint or an overstated conservative estimate
For conditional-path features (F2's yes/no, F3's yangsi/trülku), check whether the yes-path and no-path outputs have the same downstream quality requirements
Check whether any acceptance criterion within a feature is a documentation update that is not actually on the critical path for unblocking the next feature
task_context: The document decomposes four migration-blocker items into features F1 through F4 in dependency order. This review focuses on whether that decomposition correctly identifies the right features and the right boundaries — specifically whether F4's bundling inflates the critical path, whether F1's dependency on F2/F3 is overstated, and whether the conditional-path features have adequately characterised their size variance.
